rationale: Stool and mucosal biopsies (terminal ileum, rectum) have very different microbial compositions, and the published baselines differ a lot between them (~0.71 vs ~0.85). This change adds one-hot `sample_location` indicators from `meta_train`/`meta_test`, so the random forest can learn location-specific genus splits instead of mixing stool and biopsy profiles. For the external stool-only studies the indicator is constant, so it does no harm there.

Crohn's disease is consistently linked to lower gut microbial diversity (dysbiosis). Summed genus abundances cannot express that directly, so this change adds alpha-diversity features. They are OTU-level Shannon and inverse Simpson, depth-corrected expected richness rarefied to 1000 reads (computed analytically, so no random subsampling is needed), and genus-level Shannon. Because they are depth-corrected and taxonomy-agnostic, these features should also carry over to the external stool studies.

This adds the microbial dysbiosis index from the Gevers 2014 RISK paper. It is the log-ratio of the summed abundance of families that increase in Crohn's (Enterobacteriaceae, Pasteurellaceae, Fusobacteriaceae, Neisseriaceae, Veillonellaceae, Gemellaceae) to taxa that decrease (Bacteroidales, Clostridiales other than Veillonellaceae, Erysipelotrichaceae, Bifidobacteriaceae). The index and its two log-scaled parts are also added as features. Each split in the random forest looks at one genus at a time, so it cannot easily learn this multi-taxon compositional ratio. Because it is built from family and order names, it should also carry over to the external stool studies.

Right now every OTU with no genus assignment is pooled into a single `g__` column, no matter which family it belongs to. That throws away the family-level signal that matters most in Crohn's disease, where Enterobacteriaceae, Pasteurellaceae, Veillonellaceae and Fusobacteriaceae increase while Ruminococcaceae and Lachnospiraceae decrease. This change keys genera by their full lineage, so an unassigned genus stays tied to its family, and adds lineage-keyed family-level and order-level abundances. Lineage names are comparable across studies, so these features should also carry over to the external cohorts.

The random forest splits on one taxon at a time, so it captures broad compositional shifts poorly, like the coordinated loss of Clostridiales and gain of Proteobacteria and Fusobacteria in Crohn's. This change adds a second model: an L2 logistic regression on CLR-transformed genus and family abundances, keeping only taxa present in at least 5% of training samples, plus log alpha diversity and sample location. Its regularization strength is tuned by subject-grouped inner CV on the training fold. Its rank-normalized predictions are averaged with the RF's, since a linear compositional model's errors should only partly overlap with the forest's.

I'm centering the linear model's CLR and log-alpha features within each sample location, using the training-fold mean for that location. Stool, ileal and rectal communities differ much more from each other than Crohn's differs from controls. So the L2 logistic regression should judge each taxon against a same-tissue baseline rather than a pooled one, which a single location intercept can't do. The location one-hot is kept for the prior, and the external stool studies just get centered on the stool mean.

This adds a third ensemble member, a shallow LightGBM trained on the prevalence-filtered CLR genus/family features plus log-alpha diversity and location. Its rank is averaged equally with the RF and logistic model. Boosting on log-ratio features can learn tissue-specific effects and threshold rules for each taxon relative to the geometric mean. Neither the RF (which sees raw proportions) nor the additive linear model can express that, so its errors should only partly overlap with theirs.

The CLR currently adds a fixed pseudocount of 1e-5 to every relative abundance. A zero in a 3k-read sample and a zero in a 50k-read sample therefore get the same log value, even though their detection limits differ about 17-fold, so zeros are not comparable across sequencing depths. This change uses a half-read pseudocount instead (0.5 / that sample's read depth, i.e. CLR of log(counts + 0.5)), so log-ratios mean the same thing across depths in RISK and in the external studies. Read depth is added to the features only to compute this pseudocount and is kept out of both models, since it can act as a batch confounder.

The linear model will learn one shared coefficient per taxon plus a mucosal-biopsy deviation for that taxon. The biopsy indicator is 1 for terminal ileum and rectum, and the model gets both the standardized features and those features multiplied by it. Crohn's signatures differ between stool and mucosa-attached communities: biopsy signal is stronger, and some taxa, such as Enterobacteriaceae and Pasteurellaceae, shift mainly at the mucosa. A single coefficient that pools both tissues blurs this. The L2 penalty pulls the biopsy deviations toward the shared stool effect, and the stool-only external studies use just the shared coefficients.

I'm applying the same training-fold prevalence filter the logistic model uses (keep taxa present in ≥5% of training samples) to the random forest's taxon columns; alpha diversity and location stay unfiltered. Hundreds of rare genera, families and orders are nearly all zeros, and each split only samples sqrt(p) candidate features, so many splits get stuck choosing among noise taxa that won't exist in the external studies. Filtering them should make the forest split more often on the common Crohn's-relevant lineages.

This adds a per-sample "dysbiosis score", a known Crohn's signature (as in Lloyd-Price/Halfvarson). It is the median distance of the sample from the training-fold non-IBD reference samples at the same sample location, measured two ways: Bray-Curtis on genus abundances and Aitchison on genus CLR. The reference comes from the training fold only, and for training samples, reference samples from the same subject are left out. Neither model can currently express "how far is this sample from a healthy community". The RF splits on one taxon at a time and the logistic model is additive, so this whole-community distance should add new signal and should carry over to the other cohorts.

The forest currently grows trees until every leaf is pure (min_samples_leaf=1). In RISK, each subject contributes several samples, often near-duplicates (ileal and rectal biopsies, plus stool), so pure trees end up memorizing individual subjects rather than learning Crohn's composition patterns. Requiring at least 3 samples per leaf, and growing 1000 trees instead of 500 to lower variance, should give smoother, better-ranked probabilities that transfer better to new subjects and external stool cohorts.

Both models now use every taxonomic rank from genus up to phylum: class and phylum abundances are added, and the order, class and phylum blocks also go into the CLR logistic model, which previously saw only genus and family. The main Crohn's shifts are broad, like Gammaproteobacteria/Proteobacteria expansion and Clostridia/Firmicutes loss, and higher-rank sums capture them with less sparsity and noise than per-genus features. They should also transfer better to external studies, whose genus-level assignments differ.

The fixed 50/50 rank average assumes the random forest and the CLR logistic model are equally good. Round 5's +0.043 jump suggests the compositional linear model is much stronger, so equal weighting may be costing us. This change picks the blend weight using subject-grouped out-of-fold predictions inside the training fold, then shrinks it halfway toward 0.5 so a noisy estimate can't swing it too far.

Crohn's dysbiosis shows up mostly as taxa disappearing, and an additive CLR model with a pseudocount captures that poorly. Raw presence/absence would mostly track sequencing depth, so this change adds depth-normalized genus detection features to the CLR logistic model only: for each lineage-keyed genus, the analytic probability of seeing it in a 1000-read subsample (hypergeometric). These features describe presence the same way at any sequencing depth, which should help transfer to the external studies.

The forest currently splits only on raw proportions. When one taxon blooms (e.g. Enterobacteriaceae or Bacteroides), every other taxon's proportion shrinks, so proportion thresholds become unreliable. This change also gives the RF the training-fold prevalence-filtered CLR genus and family log-ratios already computed for the logistic model, so it can split on each taxon's level relative to the rest of the community, which is robust to closure.

Alpha diversity gave one of the biggest gains so far (+0.025), but every richness measure is still computed at the OTU level. De novo OTU richness is noisy and doesn't compare well across studies. This change adds depth-corrected expected richness of genera and families, both computed analytically at 1000 reads. It also adds a Faith-like taxonomic diversity: the expected number of distinct taxonomy-tree nodes from phylum down to OTU, which is like phylogenetic diversity with unit branch lengths. Losing whole lineages in Crohn's should show up more clearly in these measures than in OTU counts, and they should transfer better to the external cohorts.

The CLR logistic model uses a pure L2 penalty, so it spreads weight across hundreds of correlated, noisy genus and family log-ratios. The Crohn's signal, though, sits in a fairly small set of lineages: Enterobacteriaceae, Pasteurellaceae, Fusobacteriaceae and Veillonellaceae going up, and Clostridiales and Erysipelotrichaceae going down. This change makes the linear model an elastic net, with the L1 mix (l1_ratio in {0, 0.3, 0.6}) and C tuned jointly by the same subject-grouped inner CV. Grouping is by subject ID, so samples from one person never sit in both an inner training and inner validation fold. The L1 part should drop noise taxa, which ought to make the model sharper on RISK and transfer better to the external cohorts, where those rare taxa are often missing.

In RISK, a subject often gives several near-duplicate samples (ileal and rectal biopsies plus stool), so right now one person with three samples counts as three independent pieces of evidence and the models partly memorize those subjects. This change weights each training sample by 1/(that subject's sample count), normalized to mean 1, in both the random forest and the CLR logistic model, including the inner-CV fits used to tune C and pick the blend weight, so the models learn Crohn's patterns that hold across people.

Some known Crohn's markers act at species level, and summing to genus dilutes them. For example, *[Ruminococcus] gnavus* rises in Crohn's while *[R.] torques* falls, *Haemophilus parainfluenzae* rises, and *Faecalibacterium prausnitzii* and *Akkermansia muciniphila* fall. This change adds lineage-keyed abundances for OTUs that have an assigned species, prevalence-filtered on the training fold like the other taxa. The RF gets them as relative abundances. The logistic model gets them as log-ratios against the genus-block geometric mean, so they share the genus CLR reference. Species names are comparable across studies, so these features should also carry over to the external cohorts.
